The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Purpose: Informal communication has been ascribed well-being functions. Yet in increasingly hybrid work settings, where employees work remotely, informal exchanges frequently occur via digital channels and may hinder relational bonds and drain rather than restore employees' energy. Drawing on Communicate Bond Belong Theory, this study examines whether informal communication enhances or undermines employees' well-being in hybrid settings by considering its perceived quality, relational benefits, and energy-related costs.

Design/methodology/approach: A one-week experience sampling study (26 participants; 549 surveys) captured employees' everyday communication episodes with co-workers and their subsequent experiences. Mixed-effects models estimated within-person relationships while accounting for between-person differences.

Findings: Episodes that were more informal than usual were associated with higher striving potential (e.g., more pleasantness or meaningfulness). In turn, higher striving potential was associated with more relatedness need satisfaction and a more favorable relatedness-to-energy ratio, though not with energy expenditure. Communication modality did not moderate these associations. However, text-based (vs. audio-visual) exchanges were significantly associated with lower relatedness and energy expenditure, and a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio.

Originality: Adopting a situational perspective, this study moves beyond frequency-based and between-person approaches to everyday informal communication. It disentangles message-and channel-related effects and their distinct contributions in the relationship between informal talk and employee well-being. From this novel perspective, the findings provide evidence that informal communication is a resource for employees' well-being, but can impose demands when it occurs digitally, an aspect that practitioners should recognize when designing informal communication initiatives.

[div-01]

informal episode may not relate to well-being the same way across modalities. Given this importance of different modalities for well-being in hybrid work, we ask: How does informal communication in hybrid work contribute to, or hamper, employees' well-being?

We address this question by drawing on Hall and Davis' (2017) Communicate Bond Belong (CBB) Theory to explain how informal social interactions can promote well-being.

Based on CBB Theory, we study informal interactions and well-being through a situational lens, focusing on the quality, relational benefits, and energy-resource drawbacks of communication episodes, while also examining their modality in each encounter. A preregistered study using the experience sampling method (Beal, 2015) investigates the proposed associations in daily work life. We specify the mechanism through which informal communication supports well-being, refining this understanding by disentangling the contribution of the communication itself from that of the modality through which it occurs.

Informal communication in hybrid work settings

A common way to describe internal communication is to differentiate between its formal and informal characteristics (Koch and Denner, 2022; Kraut et al., 1990). Yet, informal communication remains a "loosely defined concept" (Kraut et al., 1990, p. 150) with 70% of all relevant articles having their own definition (Singh and Denner, 2025). Given some unresolved conceptual challenges in defining informal communication, we first outline its central characteristics and the associated definition challenges using the catalogue of Singh and Denner (2025) -actors, content, situation, and channel -and conclude with a working definition of informal communication, building upon and refining previous definitional work.

Actors. Informal communication is interpersonal talk occurring in an organizational setting between members of the organization itself (Bielenia-Grajewska, 2017). When communicating informally, employees often engage in conversations as (close) acquaintances (Koch and Denner, 2022; Methot et al., 2021). Hence, employees who are emotionally close tend to engage in more informal conversations (Kraut et al., 1990; Whittaker et al., 1994). Critically, even though informal conversations are not restricted by organizational hierarchy, the perception can diverge, as the same interaction can be more informal for one party and more formal for another: a pre-meeting talk may be relationally driven for a team member while reflecting a leadership expectation for the lead.

Content. Informal conversations have been identified as coming in various, often conceptually overlapping 'faces', such as rumor or grapevine (Crampton et al., 1998), humor or joking around (Winslow et al., 2019), small talk (Holmes, 2003), or as a specific subform like gossip (i.e., talking informally about a person not part of the conversation; Sun et al., 2023).

Typically, employees often talk about free-time activities, family, or politics (Fay, 2011; Viererbl et al., 2022). Thus, while sometimes task-related, the topics are mostly private, which previous role-based definitions often state (Koch and Denner, 2022). Informal communication can be used to acquire background knowledge about the organizational context (Denner et al., 2025), to evaluate group dynamics (Sun et al., 2023), or to serve work-related purposes in the longer term (Singh and Denner, 2025; Viererbl et al., 2021). These faces and themes imply that informal communication arises from employees' psychological needs for exchange rather than extrinsically imposed task demands.

Channels.

Informal communication used to be an activity that occurred primarily or exclusively face-to-face, as it is largely fostered by proximity (Mandhana, 2024; Whittaker et al., 1994). Yet, nowadays, many employees can be "permanently connected" to co-workers via digital technology and mobile devices during both work and non-work time (Sonnentag, 2017).

Informal communication in hybrid work settings, therefore, often occurs as computer-mediated communication (CMC), defined as "multimodal human-to-human social interaction mediated by information and communication technologies" (Meier and Reinecke, 2021, p. 1183) via private or group chats of varying modality (Begemann et al., 2024; Viererbl et al., 2021).

Situation. Most informal conversations take place at the office as a morning chat or during lunch breaks (Bielenia-Grajewska, 2017; Crampton et al., 1998), often alongside formal, scheduled meetings (e.g., "pre-meeting talk"; Allen et al., 2014), or sometimes as part of organizational etiquette or social rituals (Methot et al., 2021). According to Viererbl et al. (2022), informal conversations in remote settings occur more intentionally, as part of scheduled events, and less opportunistically. Informal communication in the office occurs frequently throughout the workday, often in brief encounters (Isaacs et al., 1997; Kraut et al., 1990; Whittaker et al., 1994). Again, a core definitional challenge is that informal communication appears fragmented throughout conversations among employees (Whittaker et al., 1994): a conversation may, for instance, start informally but then move on to a formal matter, such as pre-meeting talk (Allen et al., 2014).

Because of this fragmentation, the distinction between formal and informal communication is a continuum stretching from formal to informal interactions (Koch and Denner, 2022; Kraut et al., 1990), making informality a matter of degree, varying with the extent to which an episode is intrinsically driven rather than externally demanded, as perceived by the communicator. We locate the distinction in individuals' momentary intrinsic, relational needs for belonging and (professional) relationship building and maintenance, and within a subjective appraisal of the encounter (cf., Methot et al., 2026). We define informal communication as all interpersonal and group communication activities within an organization that are, to varying degrees, driven by employees' momentary intrinsic needs related to relationship formation or strengthening, rather than by extrinsic demands. This definition holds even when the interaction serves work-related ends as a byproduct or if the perception of informality differs between communicators, refining previous role-and goal-based definitions (Koch and Denner, 2022). The frequency, structure, and classification of informal communication are themselves shaped by boundary conditions. They can be affected by the channel (i.e., face-to-face vs. CMC), the communicators' characteristics, the content (e.g., private vs. non-private), and the situation (e.g., in-office vs. remote). These contingencies could both affect the benefits and costs of informal communication for well-being in hybrid work settings.

Informal communication and well-being: Toward an episodic lens on communication

Although the many faces of informal communication are often of interest, the qualities of the respective encounters are rarely measured. Scholars commonly assess social interaction or informal communication frequency (e.g., Denner et al., 2025; Van Zoonen and Sivunen, 2022), objective proximity (e.g., Mandhana, 2024), or app use (e.g., Carramenha et al., 2019), mostly between individuals. Such proxies register the mere occurrence of communication or its boundary conditions, e.g., channel or context (Singh and Denner, 2025), rather than the social qualities that give communication its bearing on well-being. Instead, an interpersonal communication perspective, one that researches the form and qualities of social interactions in dyads or small groups and investigates different communication occurrences within individuals, can overcome these limitations. It shifts the unit of analysis from a person's general tendencies to communication episodes such as catching up, chit-chat, or meaningful talk during everyday work life (Goldsmith and Baxter, 1996; Hall and Davis, 2017; Ledbetter et al., 2011). According to Hall (2018), communication episodes "represent the link between internal relational perceptions and manifest social behavior" (p. 4), each carrying its own relational benefits and social costs. They are thus a meaningful unit of analysis to study the different 'faces' of informal communication, such as small talk (Methot et al., 2021) or joking around (Winslow et al., 2019), across channels, communicators, and situations.

CBB Theory and the striving potential of communication episodes

Building on this interpersonal and situational view on communication, Hall and Davis' (2017) Communicate Bond Belong (CBB) Theory explains how and under which conditions different types of social interactions can lead to well-being and considers situational communication episodes as the central units of analysis. According to CBB Theory, social interaction episodes have the potential to satiate humans' intrinsic need to belong, i.e., helping humans to form and strengthen relationships with others. Feelings of relatedness, then, are the sought-after outcome of communicative behaviour and serve as a proxy for the need to belong being satisfied at a given time (Hall and Davis, 2017). However, all communication episodes typically expend energy resources (Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 38). This creates a cost-benefit relationship between social benefits and energy-related drawbacks of any daily life social interaction.

Specifically, some types of social interactions, called striving episodes, can make a particularly significant contribution to well-being by potentially satiating the need to belong more than others. Episodes that enhance bond formation or strengthening are assumed to qualify as striving behaviour. Social interactions that convey increased affection, meaningfulness, pleasantness, or self-disclosure have been classified as potentially striving, whereas, conversely, superficial, unpleasant, and impersonal interactions have been classified as potentially less striving (Hall, 2018, p. 16; Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 33).

CBB Theory thus suggests a negative association between episode frequency and the likelihood of being a striving behaviour (Hall, 2018; Hall and Davis, 2017). Consequently, humans seem to engage less frequently in communication with striving qualities than in other kinds of interpersonal talk. The authors reason this with communication episodes varying by required attention and effort (Hall, 2018) and with social interaction operating within a selfregulatory system. Specifically, because humans have a finite amount of social energy, they generally try to conserve it when possible. Hence, a high need-fulfilling potential and low energy expenditure should be the preferable type of interaction for individuals (Hall, 2018; Hall and Davis, 2017), particularly at work, where their communication activities are shaped by obligations and routines. Based on CBB Theory, informal communication should thus contribute to well-being if it comes in a shape that (a) bears high striving potential and (b) cultivates more relatedness than expending social energy.

According to the circumplex model (Methot et al., 2026), informal communication varies by interaction quality relevant to relational need satisfaction, and can be enriching but also awkward, impersonal, or exhausting at other times. We therefore treat informal communication as a potentially need-satisfying form of interaction, as any single episode may be appraised as rewarding or aversive. Yet its average striving potential should be positive for two reasons.

First, an appraisal of a communication episode can be positive regardless of an episode's 'face'.

Grounded in the need to belong (Baumeister and Leary, 1995), social contact is intrinsically rewarding because it signals connection. This underlies the core function of informal communication in developing relationships and a sense of belonging at work (e.g., Bielenia-Grajewska, 2017; Denner et al., 2025; Fay, 2011; Kim et al., 2017; Methot et al., 2026; Winslow et al., 2019). Even routine small talk that appears mundane can elevate belonging (Hall et al., 2021; Methot et al., 2021; Sandstrom and Dunn, 2014), and even normatively negative talk, such as gossip (Sun et al., 2023), can be pleasant or meaningful to the communicator. Second, because informal communication is, by our definition, more intrinsically motivated than obligatory, employees tend to exercise greater volition over when and with whom they engage in it. This selfselection should increase experienced quality, as people gravitate toward need-fulfilling and away from need-frustrating contact (Hall et al., 2021; Hall and Davis, 2017). Even where complete avoidance is difficult at work, individuals retain more autonomy in informal than formal interactions. In addition, many workplace ties take the form of "fringeships" (Fingerman et al., 2025): ties between weak and close ones, marked by mutual affection, positive in tone, and volitional in nature. These fringeships are common for work relationships and are a context in which informal communication is especially likely to be appraised as relationally rewarding.

Since we understand informal communication as varying on a continuum between being completely informal and completely formal (Koch and Denner, 2022; Kraut et al., 1990), we conceptualize the degree of 'informality' as a continuous characteristic of communication episodes. This characteristic lies at the situation level, varying from interaction to interaction.

H1: Within persons, informality of the communication episode will be positively associated with its striving potential.

Besides communication quality, informal communication should contribute to well-being if it cultivates relatedness, because feelings of relatedness are a proxy for satiating the need to belong in the present moment (Hall et al., 2023). By establishing social bonds, providing social support among co-workers, and buffering employees' stress responses (Denner et al., 2025), these striving episodes should be positively associated with feelings of relatedness, well captured by relatedness need satisfaction (Ryan and Deci, 2000).

H2: Within persons, the striving potential of communication episodes will be positively associated with employees' relatedness need satisfaction.

Additionally, Hall and Davis (2017) propose that all communication episodes typically expend energy. Episodes with a higher striving potential have been shown to occur to a lesser extent than non-striving episodes as they should require more attention and involvement (Hall, 2018) and should therefore be more depleting than episodes with less striving potential. Hence, drawing on CBB Theory's premises, the present study argues that while cultivating relatedness, episodes with higher striving potential should also expend higher social energy as a second outcome characteristic of striving episodes.

H3: Within persons, the striving potential of communication episodes will be positively associated with employees' social energy expenditure.

Finally, the cost-benefit view rooted in CBB Theory holds that informal conversation enhances well-being when its relational benefits outweigh its energy costs, a balance captured by the relatedness-to-energy ratio (Hall, 2018; Hall and Merolla, 2020). We expect striving episodes to yield a higher ratio. First, as argued above, they are appraised as more relationally rewarding, raising the relatedness benefit. Second, much striving talk is low in energetic cost: grounded in CBB Theory's energy-conservation principle, routine and familiar interactions become less effortful over time (Hall et al., 2021; Hall and Davis, 2017). Informal striving episodes are also highly recurrent in everyday work life, where their regularity makes each instance comparatively low-cost while still delivering relational benefit (Methot et al., 2021; Winslow et al., 2019). Striving episodes should thus raise relatedness without a commensurate rise in energy expenditure, consistent with Hall's (2018) finding that episodes such as joking around and expressing affection are high in the relatedness-to-energy ratio. We propose: H4foot_0 : Within persons, the striving potential of the communication episode will be positively associated with employees' relatedness-to-energy ratio.

The role of modality in hybrid work

When working remotely, not only the attributes of a communication episode but also its channel characteristics matter, as digital affordances are assumed to shape how media influence the relational and well-being outcomes of communication (Evans et al., 2017).

To understand how channel shapes communication, scholars highlight modality, which describes "how messages are delivered or presented via a medium. For example, text, graphics, sound, and video" (Bracken and Dalessandro, 2017, p. 2; Meier and Reinecke, 2021). Modality may shape a communication episode's consequences in interaction with its communicative qualities, such that the same informal exchange can yield different relational and energetic outcomes depending on how it is mediated. It thus bears on the outcomes CBB Theory identifies: relatedness, energy expenditure, and their trade-off.

Striving potential reflects the relational properties of a communication episode and is the baseline driver of its outcomes. More striving-laden talk should more strongly satisfy the need to belong, increasing relatedness, but it is also effortful and draws on energetic resources (Hall and Davis, 2017). Modality may modulate each of these relationships in different ways.

For relatedness, modality may work in opposing directions. Leaner channels convey fewer verbal and nonverbal cues, which theories from the cues-filtered-out paradigm in CMC (e.g., Media Richness; Daft and Lengel, 1986) suggest may weaken the relatedness a communication episode with striving characteristics would typically convey. Yet because remote informal communication is often more intentional, and occurs as scheduled and planned events, it skews toward the volitional, chosen episodes that CBB Theory links to greater relatedness (Hall et al., 2021). In addition, these episodes often happen with a narrower network of close ties, which would draw the relatedness upwards again (Begemann et al., 2024).

Whether modality raises or lowers the relatedness derived from striving is therefore unclear.

For energy expenditure, mediated communication may amplify the costs. Because remote informal communication must be deliberately enacted, employees must decide whether and how to initiate contact and which channel to use, which presents an effort preceding the exchange (Begemann et al., 2024; Viererbl et al., 2021). The exchange itself then imposes processing demands that rise with modality richness: cue-rich media such as video require sustained cognitive resources ("Zoom fatigue"; Bailenson, 2021), while text also taxes resources, albeit to a lesser extent. As digital informal communication typically occurs simultaneously to other activities (Begemann et al., 2024), demands should also be higher due to task-switching or multitasking.

Because modality may raise the cost of communicating, either through enactment effort, processing demands, or both, while its effect on relatedness remains uncertain, its net consequence for the relatedness-to-energy balance remains an open question. We therefore investigate how modality and the striving potential are associated with relatedness, energy expenditure, and their ratio.

RQ1: How will the striving potential of communication episodes and modality interact within-person in association with (a) relatedness need satisfaction, (b) social energy expenditure, and (c) the relatedness-to-energy ratio? Method

To match the situational and episodic focus of social interaction at work, an experience sampling study was conducted. The experience sampling method (ESM) is an intensive longitudinal design, widely used in organizational research, that includes multiple self-report measures per day to capture individuals' lived, day-to-day experience (Beal, 2015).foot_1

Participants and procedure

Twenty-six adult German-speaking employees (Mage = 32.40, SDage = 11.20, 61.5% female, 88.46% highly educated, 69.2% white-collar workers) were recruited between November and the beginning of December 2021 via convenience samplingfoot_2 . During this period, COVID-19 restrictions had eased relative to earlier lockdowns, with most participants alternating between home and office within the same week and retaining in-person social contact, conditions closer to contemporary hybrid work than to lockdown. Participants had to work at least 20 hours during the week, including at least two days of work from home, and use an Android phone to access the ESM app movisensXS. Participants were told the cover story that the study is about perceptions of flex work models. They could participate in a lottery at the end of the study period and were able to win one of four gift cards (worth 50 € each).

The study consisted of (a) an intake survey, (b) an experience sampling assessment period, and (c) an exit survey: The recruitment link incorporated the intake survey hosted on SoSciSurvey (n = 72). Before completion, participants were informed about the study procedure and asked to provide their consent. At the end of the intake, participants were instructed about and guided to the ESM app movisensXS via a personalized link (n = 55 onboardings). On the following Monday, the ESM period lasted from Monday to Friday (n = 35 ESM participants).

The exit survey, hosted on SoSciSurvey, was available after the last prompted survey on day five of the ESM period. The exit survey (n = 31) included the incentivization and a debriefing.

We collected 549 surveys (M = 21.12, SD = 6.50, Median = 24.0 surveys per participant, 85% compliance). 4 The sampling scheme was signal-contingent with semi-random intervals, i.e., random signals were sent around fixed-time surveys. Participants received five notifications per day between 9 AM and 6 PM. The number of measurement occasions per day was selected based on previous work (e.g., Methot et al., 2021; Viererbl et al., 2022). At least 60 minutes were planned between consecutive notifications. Following the initial notification, each ESM questionnaire was available for 15 minutes. According to power heuristics for twolevel nested data (Arend and Schäfer, 2019), we can reliably detect within-person effect sizes, which our study aimed to target, of a minimum size of .19-.20 with this sample size.

Measures

The intake survey assessed participants' job characteristics and sociodemographics. In the exit survey, participants self-reported their compliance during the last five workdays.

The ESM survey (M = 52.40, SD = 50.60 in seconds) measured the following constructs: Participants were first asked where they had worked during the last 60 minutes (in-office, at home, or at another place outside an office, not on duty or available to co-workers). Next, participants were asked whether they had a conversation with their co-workers or supervisors during this time, as a filter question (Hall, 2018). Informality was measured using a semantic differential scale in which participants rated how formal or informal they personally estimated the last conversation they had with their co-worker or supervisor (scale from -3 = "completely formal" to +3 = "completely informal"). Participants were then requested to indicate whether certain attributes on five continua applied to their referred conversation (Likert-type scale from -3 to +3) (Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 33). Using measures from the Rochester Interaction Record (Reis and Wheeler, 1991), participants were asked if they found the referred conversation "superficial" vs. "deep", "meaningless" vs. "meaningful", "unpleasant" vs. "pleasant", "impersonal" vs. "personal", and whether they "disclosed very little" vs. "a great deal" on the 7-point semantic differential scale, reflecting low vs. high striving potential. These five items were summarized to a mean index (α = .72). Modality was measured with a single-choice question on how the mentioned conversation took place (e.g., Bracken and Dalessandro, 2017) (choice options: face-to-face/in person, via text (e.g., in a chat, via e-mail), via audio (e.g., via phone or voice chat), audio-visual (e.g., via video call or video conference), or other).

A single-item measure of relatedness need satisfaction was taken from Reis and colleagues (Likert-type scale ranging from1 = "not at all" to7 = "extremely"; "To what extent during the mentioned conversation did you feel close and connected with the people you were with?") (Reis et al., 2000). A single item used to test CBB Theory's propositions (Hall, 2018) was considered (7-point Likert scale ranging from1 = "not at all" to7 = "extremely"; "To what degree did the mentioned conversation occupy your attention, take energy, or effort?") Some items were measured that were not part of this project (see the preregistration for details) or obtained for descriptive purposes. For instance, participants were asked on which hierarchy level the people they had the conversation with were mostly (single-choice question; options: lower, similar, higher, or different hierarchy levels).

Analysis plan

In ESM data, situational observations (level 1) are nested within individuals (level 2).

Given such a hierarchical structure, multilevel regression was applied (Hox et al., 2017). For each hypothesis and RQ1, within-person relationships were estimated while controlling for person-specific tendencies. All models were "kept maximal" (Barr et al., 2013), meaning that intercepts and slopes between participants were allowed to vary if the model converged, and that models contained within-and between-predictors and moderators. All level 1 predictors (situational level) were centered around the person mean. All level 2 predictors (person level) were centered around the sample's grand mean. For striving potential, a mean index was computed, and categorical variables were reference-coded. The relatedness-to-energy ratio was calculated by dividing each episode's relatedness score by its energy expenditure score. For the multilevel analyses, we used the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015).

Results

Means and standard deviations are displayed in Table 1. Further descriptive statistics and an overview of the changes to the preregistration are available on OSF.

As shown in Table 1, in 65.0% of all episodes (75.5% of all working episodes), participants worked from home or remotely from a location outside an office. 45.4% of all work episodes involved a social interaction, whereas this applied to 68.2% of all episodes during which participants worked away from the office. In 12.4% of all work episodes, social interaction occurred face-to-face, in 33.3% it occurred via text, in 20.1% of episodes it occurred via auditory channels, and 33.7% of all social interactions occurred audiovisually. Most commonly, participants interacted with someone at a similar hierarchical level (45.0%). On average, at least half of all social interaction episodes were rated as relatively informal.

[Table 1]

As a prerequisite for multilevel modeling, the ICCs of all situational variables were inspected. For all dependent variables, only around a third of the variance could be attributed to stable personality, sociodemographic characteristics, or traits (between .22 and .39). Multilevel modeling was deemed appropriate.

Hypothesis 1 tested the positive within-person association of informality with its striving potential at the situation level. Looking at fixed within-effects, communication episodes being more informal than usual for employees were positively and significantly associated with a communication episode's striving potential (b = .23, SE = .09, p = .016). As the model with random intercepts and slopes converged, random effects could be observed. There was substantial between-person variability in striving potential (random intercept variance τ₀₀ = 0.34) and heterogeneity in the within-person effect of informality (random slope variance τ₁₁ = 0.03), indicating that the within-person effect differed across individuals. The fixed effects explained 19.6% of the variance in striving potential (marginal R² = .196), whereas the full multilevel model, including random effects, explained 52.0% (conditional R² = .520). To conclude, Hypothesis 1 was supported by the present data.

Hypothesis 2 tested whether the striving potential of the informal communication episode would be positively associated with relatedness need satisfaction within persons. Fixed effects estimates showed that a higher striving potential than usual was significantly and positively associated with relatedness need satisfaction at the situation level (b = .67, SE = .11, p = .000). The data were therefore consistent with H2.

Hypothesis 3 tested whether striving potential positively predicted social energy expenditure within persons. Results showed that episodes with higher-than-usual striving potential were not significantly associated with social energy expenditure (b = -.28, SE = 0.15, p = .055). Therefore, H3 was rejected.

Hypothesis 4 asked how striving potential was associated with a relatedness-to-energy ratio of a communication episode. Results showed that episodes with higher-than-usual striving potential were positively and significantly associated with a higher-than-usual relatedness-to-energy ratio (b = .39, SE = .11, p = .001). This means that if employees had a social interaction with more striving qualities, the benefits of their encounter more strongly outweighed the energy-related costs. H4 was accepted.

Finally, RQ1 asked whether and how modality (i.e., text vs. audio vs. audiovisual vs. faceto-face) would interact with the striving potential of the communication episode within persons in association with (a) relatedness need satisfaction and (b) social energy expenditure, and (c) the relatedness-to-energy ratio. To obtain results, all models explaining relatedness, energy expenditure, or the relatedness-to-energy-ratio included a moderation term for striving potential and modality. Results showed no significant interaction effects, but significant simple effects for modality conditions, with audiovisual as the reference category. Compared with audiovisual interactions, text-based interactions were associated with significantly lower levels of energy expenditure (b = -1.08, SE = 0.24, p = .000) and a significantly higher relatedness-to-energy ratio (b = 0.37, SE = .18, p = .043), holding other predictors constant.

Furthermore, relative to audiovisual modality, face-to-face showed a significant increase in relatedness need satisfaction (b = 0.59, SE = .23, p = .011) and a relative decrease in energy expenditure (b = -0.93, SE = .30, p = .002). 5 However, as the prevalence of face-to-face interaction was comparably low in the sample, these results must be interpreted with caution. The significant effects together explained 45.4% of the variance in relatedness need satisfaction (marginal R² = .454), the modality effects explained 10.5% of the variance in energy expenditure (marginal R² = .105), and the fixed effects explained 20.2% in the relatedness-to-energy ratio (marginal R² = .202). There were no significant differences across the other modality conditions. See Supplement I: Table S2 in the OSF for all model estimates.

Discussion

This study advances conceptual and methodological debates on the well-being function of informal communication in hybrid work. Conceptually, prior work leaves unclear whether and by which mechanism digital informal communication confers the same benefits as face-toface, given that informal communication is held to restore employees' resources while its digital forms are presumed to deplete them. Methodologically, prior work has relied on proxies such as between-person differences in channel use or frequency, and so cannot assess whether a given episode restores or taxes resources. Drawing on CBB Theory, we move beyond whether employees communicate to how a given episode unfolds and is appraised, disentangling the contributions of communication quality from channel modality across relational benefits, energy expenditure, and their ratio. Our experience-sampling design isolates these episode-level effects from stable individual differences, a distinction prior work could not draw. Given these improvements over prior research, our results showed that informal communication is a positive experience on average, beneficial for employees' well-being. It retains its relational benefits as long as it is pleasant, deep, meaningful, and self-disclosing (H1) -even when it takes place in the work context, requires energy at the same time (H4), or occurs via more demanding modalities prevalent in hybrid work (RQ1).

The relational qualities of informal communication

On the one hand, the positive contribution of informal communication to well-being primarily builds on the positive association of informal communication with quality characteristics of communication episodes. When social interactions with co-workers or supervisors were perceived as more informal than usual, they were also more meaningful, pleasant, deep, self-disclosing, and personal, representing core characteristics of CBB Theory's striving potential. On the other hand, informal communication with more-than-usual striving characteristics also satisfied relatedness needs more than usual. Support for these associations evidences key propositions of CBB Theory: it empirically links striving attributes to CBB Theory's proposed psychological benefits of striving communication, by showing that relatedness needs are satisfied in a situation. Higher feelings of relatedness are then a "proximal indicator of the need to belong being satiated" (Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 39).

Contrary to the association between striving potential and the satisfaction of relatedness needs, striving potential was not significantly related to social energy expenditure within persons. Episodes with higher levels of meaningfulness or self-disclosure than usual, for instance, were not more energy-depleting. Hall and Davis (2017) note that the degree of energy expenditure is also "a function of familiarity with the behaviour, episode, person, and context" (p. 34).

Similar to the hidden contingencies above, energy expenditure may be explained by the extent to which informal communication is routine for employees, by the relationship with the communication partner beyond the hierarchical level, or by contextual variables (e.g., time of day or prior social contact). In daily work life, employees' capacity for informal interaction may fluctuate with workload and the amount of formal communication scheduled during the day.

Patterns of and differences in energy conservation and investment may become apparent when investigating episodes from a self-regulatory perspective, in relation to one another, and over time (e.g., Hall, 2018; Hall et al., 2023).

Given the positive within-person association between striving potential and the relatednessto-energy ratio, this means that if individuals had a social interaction at work with more striving qualities, the benefits of their encounter more strongly outweighed the energy-related costs. This is crucial for a functional perspective on informal communication (Denner et al., 2025).

Interestingly, the results showed heterogeneity in the association between informality of communication episodes and their striving potential, suggesting hidden moderators. Possible moderators could be drawn from the definition components in Singh and Denner (2025), such as actors (e.g., their relationship, their physical proximity) or the situation (e.g., the degree of volition, current workload, time of day, communication norms and culture within the organization) (for overviews, see also Begemann et al., 2024; Methot et al., 2026). For instance, disclosing personal matters may yield striving talk between very close colleagues, but feel artificial with very distant ones (e.g., Fay and Kline, 2011). Similarly, volitional and typical informal talk may strengthen relatedness where the same exchange, when imposed or ill-timed because workload is high, does not (Hall et al., 2021). This heterogeneity may also reflect distinct forms of informal communication with different functions. Methot and colleagues' (2026) circumplex model, for instance, distinguishes discrete forms varying in valence and depth -from superficial-positive talk like small talk to substantive-positive talk like meaningful conversation, which may differ in striving potential. While most episodes in our data carried striving qualities, this diversity makes the heterogeneity plausible and calls for differentiating, in future studies, between routine, superficial informal talk with a comparatively favourable relatedness-to-energy ratio and more effortful, meaningful informal talk that consumes greater energy.

The independent role of modality

Moderation analyses further revealed that striving potential and modality did not interact with relatedness, social energy expenditure, or the relatedness-to-energy ratio, which means that the relatedness benefits of communication quality are not dependent on whether informal talk occurred face-to-face, via text, via audio, or audiovisually. This is more consistent with adaptation-based accounts (Social Information Processing Theory; Walther, 1992) than with the cues-filtered-out paradigm (Daft and Lengel, 1986).

However, significant simple effects of the modality condition, text vs. audiovisual, on both outcomes have insightful implications for informal communication: When employees had a text encounter with a co-worker rather than an audiovisual one, they perceived the communication episode as less energy-consuming. This result supports the view that video-conferencing can be particularly energy-depleting (e.g., "Zoom Fatigue"; Bailenson, 2021). From a media richness perspective (Daft and Lengel, 1986), these results support the view that modalities with higher bandwidth contain more cues and can thus be more demanding for individuals than those with lower bandwidth -regardless of the informality and quality of encounters.

The finding that text-based informal interactions showed a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio than audiovisual ones suggests a trade-off between energy costs and relational benefits (Sonnentag, 2017). Consistent with CBB Theory's energy-conservation principle, which states that individuals expend the minimum energy needed to satisfy relatedness, text may offer lower energy costs while still delivering sufficient relatedness. Hall and Davis (2017, pp. 40-41) similarly speculate that text communication carries especially low energy demands, constituting a unique affordance. Text may thus be a convenient, energy-efficient means of meeting relatedness needs with co-workers, particularly relative to more demanding audiovisual formats.

Implications for CBB Theory

For interpersonal and organizational researchers as well as CMC scholars, this study extends CBB Theory by investigating part of its proposed mechanisms in a hybrid work context, where participants are also sometimes obliged to communicate more or less than preferred (Hall, 2018; Hall et al., 2021; Hall and Davis, 2017). In this regard, we may rethink the role of the workplace in CBB Theory. It has primarily treated work as a context that reshapes and often even constrains social self-regulation because workplace obligations displace optimal social contact in terms of close tie interaction, energy conservation, and relatedness needs (Hall and Davis, 2017). In addition, work talk is routine, non-volitional, and thus akin to "empty social calories" (Hall, 2018; Hall et al., 2021). Yet this rests on work talk specifically -instrumental, role-driven, largely formal -rather than the full range of communication at work, which also hosts volitional, relationally motivated episodes such as catching up or joking around (Methot et al., 2026). This complicates CBB Theory's implied dual route, in which striving typically flows from close ties but not from instrumental talk with weak ties. Relationships to co-workers typically occupy the space between (Fingerman et al., 2025), affording relatedness-beneficial communication despite an exchange context governed by professional norms.

What ultimately distinguishes the workplace, from a CBB perspective, is that relational and formal communication compete, sometimes within the same relationships and interactions.

An informal striving episode at work is thus relationship-forming talk accomplished within a formal field densely filled with impediments to energy and relatedness management. That such episodes nonetheless carry striving potential indicates that the CBB mechanism has more scope than prior work assumed: belonging can be assembled episode by episode, even within an obligation-dense context and across modalities. Plausibly, a formal, instrumental backdrop even heightens the perceived relatedness of striving exchanges, making episodes considered informal within an organization stand out more than they would in a purely social setting. This interpretation awaits empirical test, but makes concrete a suggestion in CBB Theory: that context reshapes striving (Hall and Davis, 2017).

Practical implications

For communication managers, our findings translate into three concrete recommendations: First, actively recognizing the well-being benefits of informal communication, as it is an important gateway to job satisfaction, employee health, and well-being ("the happy-productive worker" thesis; Fang et al., 2026). In practice, this means protecting informal exchange rather than treating it as time off-task. Second, create opportunities for unforced, authentic exchange among co-workers, e.g., by open recreational spaces offline or dedicated informal channels online. Because informal communication showed relational benefit which proved largely independent of channel modality, these should apply across in-office, remote, and hybrid settings and must be deliberately enabled. Employees, particularly during onboarding, need organizational support for this initiation. Our study thus suggests caution in treating face-to-face as a "gold standard" requiring employees to "come back to the office" at all costs. Third, balance such opportunities against employees' limited energy, as modalities differ in the effort they require. For instance, fewer mandatory meetings or video-conferences can protect the resources that meaningful informal exchange depends on, whereas text-based channels have a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio and may thus aid employees to balance multiple demands during their workday.

Limitations and future perspectives

Even though this is the first study to investigate informal communication and well-being in hybrid work from a situational perspective, some caveats need to be acknowledged. First, the small sample size was sufficient for the preregistered within-person tests (Arend and Schäfer, 2019; see methods section) but did not permit robust estimation of between-person effects. Our within-person sample was also somewhat smaller than comparable studies, so results should be interpreted cautiously and replicated with larger samples. Future studies should adopt broader recruitment, such as partnering with organizations or panel providers. Additionally, compliance was reduced by challenges inherent to ESM in employee samples, as prompts may interrupt work tasks or meetings, leading participants to silence devices and miss surveys. To mitigate this, we recommend multimodal prompting (e.g., smartphone plus desktop).

Second, we relied on single items from prior work, which are indispensable in situ but warrant systematic validation. Informality was assessed via a semantic differential (matching the informality continuum; Koch and Denner, 2022; Kraut et al., 1990), well-suited to ESM but potentially oversimplifying shifts within a single interaction. We deliberately did not provide participants with a definition of informal communication to remain inclusive toward novel re-

Conclusion

Hybrid work has become the "new normal". Organizations now navigate the back-tooffice movement alongside concerns about a "loneliness epidemic" that also affects relationships at work. In this context, the present study examines the mechanisms of the well-being function of informal communication in everyday hybrid work, advancing understanding of its functional role for employees and organizations (Denner et al., 2025). We show that informal communication can support high-quality exchanges among co-workers and thus employee well-being. Yet digital communication may not be uniformly beneficial, as high-bandwidth formats, in particular, also draw on employees' limited social energy. Informal communication should thus emphasize its recreational function and not be a further source of strain. Continued longitudinal and situational research is crucial to understand how employees navigate a world of permanent digital connectedness while remaining healthy and engaged -an ongoing issue for social scientists, communication managers, and public health advocates alike.

mote episodes, which an office-based definition might exclude. While necessary given the limited literature at the time, this may have introduced heterogeneity in what participants counted as informal. Future work should test whether a shared definition sharpens measurement without increasing burden. Similarly, participants reported the main modality of their most recent interaction, although workplace communication is often multimodal (McEwan, 2021). Rapid modality shifts (e.g., voice memo followed by text within a messenger) may be difficult to recall. Still, the present ESM design reduces recall bias compared to cross-sectional survey designs and provides a step toward understanding informal communication in daily work contexts. More granular results may be obtained by behavior observation or tracking. Third, the study could not fully address several contingencies and temporal self-regulation dynamics emphasized in informal communication research and CBB Theory. It offers limited insight into sociodemographic factors, traits, and job characteristics, although the withinperson design controlled for stable individual differences and ICCs indicated small betweenperson variance. Still, the sample overrepresented younger, highly educated white-collar employees. Given potential age-related differences in technological competence, older employees may experience digital informal communication as more energy-taxing, for instance. Future research should use more diverse samples, examine situational boundary conditions, and could trace CBB Theory's self-regulatory dynamics through sequential, causal analyses of episodes across workdays.
